paras: The tarring and feathering of Paul Ellis took place on the night of July 6, 1882, in Shrewsbury, Vermont, when fifteen to twenty-five men put a rope around his neck at a tree, threatened to hang him, and coated him with tar and feathers. The men accused Ellis of an attempted assault on a fourteen-year-old girl, a charge a justice soon dismissed for lack of evidence. Papers noted that a justice of the peace and wealthy farmers led the mob, and in October the participants pleaded guilty and paid $12.50 each.

Ellis was a farm laborer of about fifty, described by Vermont papers as a drunken man separated from his wife, and by the Sun as a good farmhand who earned high wages. Charles Gleason, a poor Shrewsbury farmer who owed Ellis money, said that on June 19 Ellis attempted to assault his daughter while she churned, and also charged Ellis with stealing $5. Ellis denied the charge, saying the girl had asked him to help her churn and that Gleason turned on him after he refused to lend more money.

According to the Sun's Rutland correspondent, Gleason three times threatened Ellis with a knife, the lynching was first planned for Wednesday night but put off for want of men, and on Thursday Gleason bought tar in Rutland.

About ten o'clock on Thursday night the party surrounded the house of Timothy Coakley, where Ellis had just arrived to start work the next day, and over Coakley's objection men entered and tied a rope around his waist. They dragged him more than half a mile down the road to a tree, moved the rope to his neck, threw the other end over a limb, and told him to prepare for death. Ellis said he was pulled up several times and threatened unless he confessed; he admitted petty thefts but not the assault, and was then tarred and feathered and turned loose in the woods on a promise to leave.
Instead of leaving, Ellis went to Rutland, where he met the justice who had led the mob and was arrested for drunkenness on Saturday, July 8.

Examined before Justice Bailey on the charge of assaulting Julia Gleason, Ellis was discharged because the evidence was not sufficient to hold him. Six men, Henry W. Wilcox, Henry Plumley, John Danvers, Charles Gleason, Patrick Dyer and Addison Pierce, were arrested, waived examination, and were bound over in $250 each, one of them a justice of the peace.

In late September a grand jury indicted those six and two more, Charles Dyer and George Butterfly, for tarring and feathering Ellis. In the Rutland County Court each defendant pleaded guilty and was required to pay $12.50.

The New York Sun carried the fullest account under the headline 'Lynch Law in Vermont', reporting that the lynchers seemed proud of their exploit and that investigation made the alleged assault 'somewhat questionable'. Its correspondent added that people in Rutland and Shrewsbury upheld the lynchers because of Ellis's poor character and their wealth, while the local daily demanded their punishment; a Baltimore German paper translated the same dispatch.

Vermont weeklies reprinted a Rutland Herald version that stated the attempted rape as fact, called the episode 'Almost a Lynching', and described Ellis as 'a drunken, dissipated man'. Later Vermont and New Hampshire items reported his discharge flatly, the Concord paper stating that 'There was no evidence against Ellis.'

Beyond New England, the Springfield Republican called it 'a genuine case of lynch law' and noted doubts about the girl's story, the Eureka Sentinel in Nevada judged Ellis probably innocent, and the San Antonio Evening Light mocked the crowd for settling on tar and feathers. No article in the coverage mentions Ellis's race.

Whether Ellis was actually hoisted is disputed: he said he was pulled up a number of times, and the Springfield Republican said his feet cleared the ground, but the lynchers told the Sun they only threatened him. The Rutland Herald version also differs on the sequence, placing the tar and feathers before a rail ride to a nearby tree, and early items said Ellis left for parts unknown, which later reports of his Rutland arrest contradict.

reader.title: Tarring and feathering of Paul Ellis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A band of 15 to 25 men seized Paul Ellis on an accusation of attempted assault on a girl, put a rope around his neck at a tree and threatened to hang him, then tarred and feathered him and let him go (A1, A5, A10); he survived, so it was at most an attempted lynching.

Ellis was not killed: he was released and turned up in Rutland the next days (A1, A6), though a group of 15 to 25 men acting without legal authority on an accusation of attempted rape threatened to hang him (A1, A5, A10).

The Rutland dispatch to the Sun (A1), the Rutland Herald account reprinted in Vermont (A5, A7, A8) and the Springfield Republican (A10) agree on the seizure, rope, threat to hang and tar and feathers, and later court items confirm arrests, indictments and guilty pleas (A13, A20, A29).

accounts.label: Ellis's version
accounts.gist: He was pulled up several times and threatened with death unless he confessed; the girl asked him to help churn, and Gleason accused him because Ellis refused to lend more money.

accounts.label: Lynchers' version
accounts.gist: They talked freely of the act and said they had only threatened to hang him.

accounts.label: Rutland Herald account
accounts.gist: Stated the assault as fact; the mob tarred and feathered Ellis at a neighbor's, carried him on a rail to a nearby tree, and released him on a promise to leave.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Lynch Law in Vermont' and 'Little Evidence of the Victim's Guilt', reported the lynchers' pride and questioned the accusation.
The Rutland Herald account reprinted in Vermont weeklies treated the attempted rape as fact and described Ellis as 'a drunken, dissipated man'.
The Springfield Republican called it 'a genuine case of lynch law' and Ellis 'the poor wretch', noting the girl's story was doubted.
Later court notices and the Eureka Sentinel reported the discharge, indictments and fines, the Sentinel saying Ellis was probably innocent.
The San Antonio Evening Light mocked the episode, saying the crowd wanted 'a good honest lynching' but settled for tar and feathers.

info: Thursday night about 10 o'clock, before a Rutland dispatch dated July 8, 1882, i.e. July 6, 1882
Seized at the house of Timothy Coakley, a farmer of Shrewsbury, a mountain town about a dozen miles east of Rutland; taken over half a mile down the road to a tree
Paul Ellis, a farm laborer about fifty years old; no paper states his race
Accused of attempted criminal assault on the fourteen-year-old daughter of Charles Gleason (named as Julia Gleason) on June 19; Ellis denied it
A justice of the peace, well-to-do farmers of Shrewsbury and the girl's father, Charles Gleason; six named in arrests and eight in indictments
Justice Bailey discharged Ellis on the assault charge for insufficient evidence
